Astrophysics

 Home Physics Branches of physics
OurBigBook.com Words: 112k Articles: 2k
Astrophysics uses physics to explain stars, planets, galaxies, and their electromagnetic radiation; cosmology extends the questions to the universe as a whole. Much of its evidence arrives as light. The challenge is to infer the source's physical properties from what reaches an observer: a bright star might be nearby, unusually luminous, or both. Stellar parallax and observed radiative flux make this distinction quantitative.
This is an inverse problem. A forward problem predicts observations from a source model and the intervening radiative transfer; the inverse problem works backwards from observations to possible models. A spectral line can constrain chemical elements, temperature, and motion through the Doppler effect, but its strength also depends on the stellar atmosphere. Combining different measurements is therefore more informative than interpreting brightness alone. The attraction is that a tiny change in the direction of light can supply a distance, turning received radiative flux into intrinsic luminosity. [ref].

Gamma-ray burst

Words: 46
Astrophysics OurBigBook.com
A brief, intense transient of gamma-ray emission from an astrophysical source. Short bursts include events powered by compact-star mergers, while many long bursts are associated with massive-star collapse. Jet structure and viewing geometry affect observed luminosities. GW170817 connected one short burst directly to a neutron-star merger.

Astrophysical jet

Words: 368 Articles: 6
Astrophysics OurBigBook.com
A collimated plasma outflow from an astrophysical engine, often associated with accretion. Magnetic stresses, rotation, pressure and interaction with an external medium shape its acceleration and confinement. Jets can carry particle kinetic energy, thermal energy and electromagnetic energy far beyond the compact launch region.

Relativistic jet

Words: 327 Articles: 5
Astrophysical jet OurBigBook.com
A jet with bulk velocity sufficiently close to the speed of light that relativistic aberration, frequency shifts and arrival-time effects strongly affect its appearance. The moving emitting pattern need not track the speed of every plasma component.

Gamma-ray compactness problem

Words: 195 Articles: 2
Relativistic jet OurBigBook.com
Rapidly varying high-energy sources can appear too dense in target photons to transmit their observed gamma rays. For an approximately isotropic stationary region with target-band luminosity L2​, radius R and target photon energy ϵ2​, the target number density is n∼L2​/(4πR2cϵ2​). photon-photon pair production then gives optical depth τ∼nσR. A luminosity variability size bound can make this very large. relativistic beaming both increases the inferred rest-frame size and reduces the inferred rest-frame radiation density, allowing escape. This radiation-opacity argument is distinct from gravitational stellar compactness and topological compactness.

Astrophysics OurBigBook.com
For luminosity L, mass-energy equivalence gives ∣M˙∣=L/c2. Holding L constant gives a time t=fMc2/L to radiate a mass fraction f. A blackbody estimate uses the Stefan–Boltzmann law, L=4πR2σT4. This is a radiative-energy estimate, not a model of a star's evolving nuclear fuel or mass loss in a wind.

Point-like astronomical source

Words: 62
Astrophysics OurBigBook.com
A point-like astronomical source has an angular extent negligible for the calculation or measurement being considered. The ideal mathematical limit concentrates its luminosity at one source-plane position. In gravitational lensing, this approximation permits divergent formal magnifications on a caustic; a finite source averages the magnification over its emitting area. An unresolved source need not have negligible size compared with the lens's caustic scale.

Stellar parallax (p, ϖ)

Words: 576 Articles: 4
Astrophysics OurBigBook.com
Stellar parallax is the apparent change in a star's viewing direction caused by the observer's changing position. Nearby stars shift more against a distant reference background. In an ideal circular Earth orbit, the conventional annual stellar parallax p uses a baseline of one astronomical unit, approximately the Earth-Sun distance. Two opposite observing positions, about six months apart, are separated by approximately two astronomical units. Their maximum angular separation is 2p, so p is half that excursion, not the full January-to-July shift. The observed excursion depends on the projected baseline and observing dates. [ref].
For the perpendicular baseline in the diagram, a right triangle gives
tanp=d1au​,d=tanp1au​≃p1au​,
(2)
where p in the final expression is in radians. Combining the small-angle approximation with the parsec convention gives
1pcd​≃p/(1arcsec)1​.
(3)
Thus p=0.05 arcseconds implies d≃20 parsecs, while the ideal six-month excursion is 0.10 arcseconds. Geometry supplies this distance without assuming a luminosity or a particular stellar atmosphere.
In practical astrometry, many observations separate the annual stellar parallax signal from proper motion, the star's own changing sky position. The Gaia DR3 catalogue reports stellar parallax and its uncertainty in milliarcseconds: 50mas=0.05 arcseconds. A catalogue angle is a fitted measurement with measurement error. [ref].
For a positive stellar parallax with small standard deviation σp​, first-order propagation gives σd​/d≃σp​/p. Thus p=50mas with σp​=1mas gives d≃20 parsecs with σd​≃0.4 parsecs, assuming systematic offsets are negligible. This linear estimate requires σp​≪p; a reciprocal is nonlinear and does not generally preserve symmetric uncertainty intervals.

Stellar parallax OurBigBook.com
For a Gaussian measured stellar parallax, the likelihood at distance r approaches a nonzero constant as r→∞. An unbounded spatial-volume prior proportional to r2 therefore gives an improper posterior. A finite survey/population model or a decaying density is needed. The illustrative proper prior displayed has normalizing constant 1/(2L3); its scale is a model choice requiring justification, not a new measured datum. prior sensitivity is especially important at low parallax signal-to-noise.

Lutz-Kelker bias (p(ϖ)∝ϖ−4 for a locally uniform spatial population)

Stellar parallax OurBigBook.com
The classical parallax-calibration problem combines measurement errors with the greater volume available at larger distances. A locally uniform spatial population has p(r)∝r2, which transforms under r=1/ϖ to p(ϖ)∝ϖ−4 on the valid distance interval. Parallax cuts and the nonlinear conversion to luminosity can bias calibration samples. A correction is not universal: the population model, selection information and inferential target must be specified. Distinguish the repeated-sampling bias of a selected sample from inference for a particular star using a justified prior.[ref]

Parsec (pc)

Stellar parallax OurBigBook.com
The parsec is a distance unit defined by the exact convention
1pc=π648000​au≃3.085677581×1016m.
(4)
The astronomical unit is exactly 149597870700m; one arcsecond is exactly π/648000 radians. The IAU resolution explicitly records the parsec convention. A megaparsec is one million parsecs. [ref]. [ref].
The familiar description "the distance giving one arcsecond of stellar parallax" uses the small-angle approximation. Exact right triangle geometry instead gives au/tan(π/648000), slightly shorter than the conventional parsec. The relative difference is approximately (π/648000)2/3≃7.83×10−12. This is negligible for the examples here, but distinguishing an exact unit convention from an approximate geometric interpretation prevents a misleading equality.

Intergalactic medium (IGM)

Words: 2k Articles: 8
Astrophysics OurBigBook.com
The intergalactic medium is the gas between galaxies. Its diffuse, ionized component contains much of the ordinary matter outside stars. Lyman-alpha absorption measures its small neutral-hydrogen fraction, while hotter phases require other tracers.

Temperature-density relation of photoionized intergalactic gas (T=T0​(1+δ)γ−1)

Words: 55
Intergalactic medium OurBigBook.com
Diffuse gas in photoionization equilibrium is often approximately described by the displayed temperature-density contrast relation. Photoheating and expansion cooling produce its thermal history. It is an empirical model for low-density gas, not the adiabatic equation of state of every intergalactic phase. Lyman-alpha forest line widths constrain both the temperature at a reference density and the slope through their lower envelope.

Cosmic ionizing background (Jν​)

Words: 35
Intergalactic medium OurBigBook.com
The cosmic ionizing background is the diffuse radiation field capable of photoionization of intergalactic gas. Its specific intensity depends on source luminosity functions, ionizing photon escape fractions, cosmological redshifting, and radiative transfer through absorbers. Quasars and star formation supply major contributions with different spectral shapes and evolution.

Lyman-alpha forest

Words: 2k Articles: 5
Intergalactic medium OurBigBook.com
The Lyman-alpha forest is the multitude of foreground Lyman-alpha absorption features in a distant quasar's spectrum, at wavelengths shorter than its own redshifted Lyman-alpha emission. The quasar supplies a bright background; intervening neutral hydrogen atoms remove photons near their local Lyman-alpha line resonance. Many dips can therefore come from one atomic transition encountered at different redshifts, rather than from many different chemical elements. Some features are instead transitions of other ions, so a dip alone does not identify Lyman-alpha absorption. This makes faint foreground gas detectable through the light it removes, even when its own emission would be difficult to see. [ref].
Ignoring peculiar velocity for the moment, an absorber at cosmological redshift za​ puts its Lyman-alpha line at
λobs​=λα​(1+za​),za​=λα​λobs​​−1,λα​=1215.67A˚.
(5)
The rest wavelength is in the ultraviolet; at za​=2 it appears at 3647.01A˚ in the optical spectrum. In a toy sightline to a quasar at zQ​=3, absorbers at za​=2, 2.35, 2.7 appear at 3647.01, 4072.4945, 4497.979A˚, all shortward of the quasar's Lyman-alpha emission position 4862.68A˚. The absorbing atoms see the selected photons at their own resonance; the observed dip's redshift belongs to the foreground gas. Peculiar velocity adds a Doppler shift, so the inferred za​ is not a pure distance coordinate. The rest wavelength and resonance interpretation are given in Rauch (1998), section 1.
The diagram uses invented optical depths and 26 Doppler cores; three selected foreground regions are marked. Their drawn positions and sizes are schematic. The dashed comparison imposes a uniform optical depth τ=2, giving transmission e−2≃0.135 throughout the chosen foreground band. It is an idealized smooth-absorption model, not a measured spectrum or a prediction of the actual intergalactic medium.
The smooth comparison explains the Gunn-Peterson effect: neutral hydrogen distributed throughout an expanding intergalactic medium can absorb continuously over a wavelength interval, because different parts of the path resonate with different observed wavelengths. The resolved Lyman-alpha forest instead has strong transmission fluctuations and distinguishable absorption lines. These need not represent isolated compact clouds: diffuse sheets and filaments in the cosmic web can generate peaks in optical depth along one line of sight. A continuously varying gas distribution can look like a collection of lines. [ref]. [ref].
An early observation makes the identification concrete. Lynds's 1971 paper analyzed six spectrograms of the quasar 4C 05.34, with emission redshift 2.877, taken in spring 1970 using an image-tube spectrograph on Kitt Peak's 84-inch telescope. Five covered 3200–7500A˚ with approximately 10A˚ resolution; the most informative covered about 3500–6000A˚ at 5A˚ resolution. Its reproduced spectrogram shows the strong Lyman-alpha emission flanked mostly on the short-wavelength side by numerous absorption lines. Lynds tabulated their wavelengths and estimated strengths, identified five absorption redshift systems, and proposed that many remaining unidentified lines were the same Lyman-alpha line at additional redshifts. He explicitly warned about blending, an incomplete census of weak lines, and wavelength errors around 0.5–1A˚. The result established a striking spectral pattern; the paper's proposed interpretation did not measure a separate physical cloud for every dip. [ref].
A contrasting observation demonstrates smooth, very strong absorption. Becker and collaborators (2001) used the Echelle Spectrograph and Imager on Keck II to observe the quasar SDSSp J103027.10+052455.0 at zQ​=6.28. Sky lines gave an instrumental full width at half maximum of about 1.8A˚ near 8500A˚, or spectral resolving power R≃4700. After sky subtraction and flux calibration, the mean continuum-normalized transmission over 8450–8710A˚ was 0.0038±0.0026, consistent with zero; this corresponds to absorption redshifts approximately 5.95–6.16. They identified a Gunn-Peterson trough. Crucially, resonant Lyman-alpha absorption is so sensitive that even a small neutral fraction can make transmission undetectable: the trough alone does not establish a mostly neutral intergalactic medium or uniquely date reionization. [ref].
What a spectrum constrains is a radiative transfer problem. For an ideal foreground screen with negligible emission into the observed beam, the intrinsic continuum-normalized transmission is
T(λ)=Fcont​(λ)F(λ)​=e−τ(λ),NHI​=∫nHI​dℓ.
(6)
Here F is spectral radiative flux, Fcont​ is its unabsorbed continuum, τ is optical depth, nHI​ is neutral hydrogen number density, and NHI​ is neutral hydrogen column density along proper path length ℓ. A Voigt profile model constrains redshift, column density and a velocity width together. A nearly black line has lost much of its sensitivity to further increases in optical depth; blending and an uncertain continuum can also admit different fitted components. Finite spectral resolving power and noise limit which widths and weak features can be measured. [ref]. [ref].
For a purely thermal Doppler core, use the velocity convention τ(v)∝exp[−(v−v0​)2/b2]. The Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution then gives
bth​=mH​2kB​T​​≃12.85104KT​​kms−1,
(7)
where kB​ is the Boltzmann constant, T is temperature and mH​ is a hydrogen atom's mass. This b is 2​ times the Gaussian distribution's standard deviation. Higher temperature spreads the same column density over more velocities. An instrument also broadens a line: locally, for a nearly flat continuum, the recorded transmission is approximately the convolution of T with the normalized instrumental response, not the exponential of a convolved optical depth. A Gaussian response with full width at half maximum c/R has standard deviation c/[R8log2​], where c is the speed of light and R the spectral resolving power.
The upper model fixes the integral ∫τ(v)dv, hence the neutral hydrogen column density for this transition, while changing temperature. A cooler line blurred by an instrument resembles a warmer intrinsic line. The lower model has two equal Doppler cores separated by 24kms−1: reducing spectral resolving power merges them into one apparent feature. Both panels use invented profiles, Gaussian instrumental responses, and no noise or damping wings. They illustrate an inverse problem, rather than measurements of temperature or a universal relation between a dip and a cloud.
Better observations provide the inputs to that inverse problem. Kim, Cristiani and D'Odorico (2001) analyzed three quasars with the VLT's UVES spectrograph. For HE2217–2818, Table 1 records zQ​=2.413 and 16200s of exposure in the 3050–3860A˚ setup in October 1999. Isolated thorium-argon lamp lines measured R≃45000; the data were resampled into 0.05A˚ bins, with signal-to-noise ratios about 45–50 per pixel over 3550–4050A˚. They fitted a local polynomial continuum, fitted Voigt profiles, and compared statistics of the transmitted flux. Their analysis excluded the region near the quasar to avoid the quasar proximity effect and used the interval between its Lyman-beta and Lyman-alpha emission to reduce confusion with other Lyman-series absorption. Features below NHI​=1012.5cm−2 became confused with noise, setting their adopted lower column density limit. Figure 1 shows the measured spectrum, fitted profiles and residuals. This was a calibrated absorption measurement, with explicit selection limits. [ref].
Even after instrumental correction, a width need not be purely thermal Doppler broadening. Hubble flow across extended gas, peculiar velocity structure and unresolved blends can contribute. If an isolated line's intrinsic width obeys b2=bth2​+bnt2​ with an independent Gaussian nonthermal contribution bnt2​≥0, then T≤mH​b2/(2kB​); b=25kms−1 gives a computed upper bound about 3.79×104K. A complex blend need not satisfy this single-component model. Noise can also bias the fitted widths of weak lines. This is why the thermal cutoff of Lyman-alpha line widths, calibrated against gas models, is more informative than assigning a temperature to every dip. [ref].
Finally, neutral hydrogen column density is not total gas mass density. In a pure hydrogen approximation, with gas optically thin to ionizing radiation and nearly fully ionized in photoionization equilibrium, the Lyman-alpha forest photoionization scaling gives
nHI​≃Γα(T)nH2​​,xHI​≃Γα(T)nH​​,
(8)
where nH​ counts all hydrogen nuclei, Γ is the photoionization rate, α(T) is the radiative recombination coefficient and xHI​=nHI​/nH​ is the neutral fraction. At fixed temperature and Γ, doubling nH​ quadruples nHI​; doubling Γ halves it. These computed examples explain both the sensitivity to density contrast and the ambiguity: stronger absorption can mean denser gas, weaker ionizing radiation, a different temperature, or more path length. The Jeans-length ionization correction for the Lyman-alpha forest adds a size model rather than an independently measured depth. Optically thick Lyman limit systems and damped Lyman-alpha systems require different treatment. [ref]. [ref].
The beauty of the Lyman-alpha forest is that a spectrum converts otherwise faint foreground gas into a sequence of markers through cosmic time. With a model of radiative transfer, velocities, ionizing radiation and the temperature-density relation of photoionized intergalactic gas, its transmission statistics probe the cosmic web and gas thermal history. A single line of sight remains one narrow sample, not a unique three-dimensional density map. [ref].

Gas density, temperature, ionizing radiation and path length are all required to infer a baryon density from Lyman-alpha absorption.

Then NHI​≃α(T)nH2​L/Γ∝[α(T)/Γ](fg​T)1/2nH3/2​. Solving for nH​ and substituting in NH​=nH​L gives the displayed correction. Thus the ionized mass integral weights the neutral-hydrogen column-density distribution by NHI1/3​ rather than NHI​. Redshift evolution of the Lyman-alpha forest

Words: 73
Lyman-alpha forest OurBigBook.com
The Lyman-alpha forest becomes denser and more opaque towards higher cosmological redshift, for a fixed absorption selection over the ordinary post-reionization range. The incidence is often parametrized as dN/dz=A(1+z)γ, with the index depending on the column density threshold and epoch. The evolution flattens at low redshift as the declining cosmic ionizing background partly offsets dilution of the intergalactic medium. For optically thin gas at fixed overdensity, photoionization equilibrium gives approximately nHI​∝α(T)(1+z)6/Γ, illustrating why density, temperature and ionizing radiation all matter.

Proximity effect (astrophysics)

Words: 139 Articles: 1
Lyman-alpha forest OurBigBook.com
The quasar proximity effect is a reduction of nearby Lyman-alpha forest absorption caused by extra photoionization from the quasar. At fixed density and temperature in photoionization equilibrium, an added rate ΓQ​ changes the neutral fraction by the factor Γbg​/(Γbg​+ΓQ​). A host environment with positive density contrast can mask this reduction, and a variable or anisotropic source complicates its interpretation.
Proximity-effect estimator of the ionizing background (NHI​=NHI(0)​/(1+ω),ω=ΓQ​/Γbg​)
Words: 83
Proximity effect (astrophysics) OurBigBook.com
In photoionization equilibrium at fixed gas density and temperature, the extra quasar photoionization rate reduces neutral-hydrogen column density by the displayed factor. Its local rate is calculated from the quasar flux, while the isotropic background rate is Γbg​=4π∫Jν​σHI​(ν)/(hν)dν. Fitting the absorption suppression versus proper distance constrains the cosmic ionizing background. For an unperturbed column-density distribution proportional to N−p with p>1, the line abundance above a fixed threshold is reduced by (1+ω)1−p. Density enhancement, quasar age, anisotropy and redshift errors must be distinguished from this ionization effect.

Photoevaporation

Words: 283 Articles: 4
Astrophysics OurBigBook.com
Radiation heats gas sufficiently to drive an escaping thermal outflow. It can remove material from protoplanetary disks, planetary atmospheres and irradiated clouds. In a heated Keplerian disk, the photoevaporative gravitational radius compares the sound speed with the orbital speed. The mass-loss rate depends on the heating, density and wind geometry rather than radiation pressure alone.

A horizontal coordinate system describes a viewing direction using altitude γ above the observer's astronomical horizon and azimuth η around it. Here azimuth starts at true north and increases through east: north is 0∘, east 90∘, south 180∘, and west 270∘, with 0≤η<360∘. True north is the northward intersection of the celestial meridian with the astronomical horizon, rather than an uncorrected magnetic-compass reading. Other origins and directions are legitimate, but their formulae must be converted consistently. [ref].
Construct a local orthonormal basis of east eE​, north eN​, and upward eU​, with eE​×eN​=eU​. The upward unit vector points to the zenith; the horizontal plane is perpendicular to it. For a ground instrument, a freely hanging weight establishes the local vertical through gravity. In an elementary spherical-Earth model, this vertical is radial; precision work distinguishes it from the normal to a reference surface. With the observer as origin, write a direction's unit vector as
n=cosγsinηeE​+cosγcosηeN​+sinγeU​.
(10)
Its local components (E,N,U) obey E2+N2+U2=1. Conversely, γ=arcsinU and η=atan2(E,N) modulo one turn, except where E=N=0. The quadrant-aware arctangent takes east as its first argument and north as its second. A synthetic direction with η=60∘ and γ=30∘ has (E,N,U)=(3/4,3​/4,1/2). Thus its horizontal component has norm 3​/2; its altitude is not the angle of the projected arrow in the horizontal plane.
A horizontal coordinate system depends on the observer's site and the observation time. The Earth's rotation changes the local axes relative to a fixed distant direction, while changing the site changes the zenith and the astronomical horizon. This makes the horizontal coordinate system directly useful for pointing an optical telescope and checking whether terrain blocks a target. A pair of angles without a site, time, azimuth convention, and geometric or refracted interpretation is an incomplete pointing instruction.
For a check against an equatorial coordinate system, let θ be the observer's geographical latitude, δ the direction's declination, and h its west-positive hour angle, obtained from local sidereal time minus right ascension. In the spherical-Earth, unrefracted fixed-direction model, projection onto the local orthonormal basis gives
E=−cosδsinh,N=cosθsinδ−sinθcosδcosh,U=sinθsinδ+cosθcosδcosh.
(11)
Taking the dot product with the upward unit vector gives the last formula; the other two follow by the same projection. Recover altitude and azimuth from (E,N,U) as above, using radians inside software trigonometric functions. The minus sign in E is essential: a negative hour angle puts this synthetic direction east of the celestial meridian. [ref].
For illustrative geographical latitude θ=45∘ and invented declination δ=15∘, hour angle h=−60∘ gives γ≃31.636∘ and η≃100.729∘. At h=+60∘, the same altitude accompanies η≃259.271∘: the direction is now westward. At h=0, it is due south with altitude 60∘, agreeing with 90∘−∣θ−δ∣ at upper meridian transit. These are analytical checks, not present positions of any star. For nearby objects, the direction must also be referred to the observer; simply rotating a geocentric direction omits the change of viewing position. Catalogue-to-observation refinements are described under equatorial coordinate system.

Altitude γ, also called elevation angle, is the signed angle from the astronomical horizon to a viewing direction, measured in the vertical plane containing that direction and the zenith. Its range is −90∘≤γ≤90∘: positive altitude is above the horizontal plane, zero altitude lies on the astronomical horizon, and 90∘ points to the zenith. Altitude measures direction, rather than a Euclidean distance or a height in metres. In the local horizontal coordinate system, sinγ=n⋅eU​; the dot product makes the sign unambiguous even for directions below the astronomical horizon.
A concrete motivating observation is the Exploratorium Teacher Institute's Height Sight activity. Its inclinometer uses a sighting tube fixed to a card and an angular scale, with a string and small weight hanging from the scale's pivot. A partner reads where the freely hanging string meets the scale. Sighting a level target should give a readout near zero; sighting a taller target gives an angular height. The activity asks the observer to move closer and farther: the closer position gives the larger angle. The interpretation is that the readout measures the tube's tilt relative to the gravity reference, while converting that angle to a physical height also requires distance and eye height. The activity also extends the inclinometer to sky observations. [ref].
The following calibration and sky sequence is a proposed extension, with no claimed observing dataset. First establish two reference marks at the same height with a water level, rather than assuming that a sloping floor or distant ridge is horizontal. Keep the inclinometer in a vertical plane, sight between the marks, wait for the weight to settle, and read the zero several times. Next sight a mark whose independently measured rise q above the tube and horizontal separation d are known; a right triangle predicts γref​=arctan(q/d). A synthetic q=3m, d=5m gives γref​=30.964∘. Checking both zero and this nonzero angle can reveal a wrongly attached tube or a scale read from the wrong end. Use level separation, not distance along inclined ground.
If the scale's indicated altitude is m=γapp​+b, estimate its additive zero b from the level sight, then obtain apparent altitude γapp​=m−b. For synthetic readings b=1.0∘ and m=32.0∘, the corrected altitude is 31.0∘, close to the 30.964∘ calibration prediction. Declaring illustrative readout bounds of 0.5∘ for each reading gives a conservative combined bound of 1.0∘ on m−b; these bounds are assumptions, not measured performance. Repeatability tests the variation between readings, whereas a persistent zero offset remains a systematic measurement error. Include uncertainty in the reference rise and separation before judging agreement.
At a fixed site, sight a recognizable star, record the observation time, corrected altitude and north-through-east azimuth, and repeat over a short interval. Record the terrain boundary at the same azimuth separately from the gravity-defined zero. The fixed-direction model in horizontal coordinate system predicts changing angular readouts as the Earth rotates; this is a prospective test, rather than a fabricated measurement curve. Keep the tube aligned, the string free of contact and shielded from wind, the eye at the same reference position, and repeat the level check afterward. Timestamp each sight so genuine sky motion is not mistaken for poor repeatability. An optical telescope with an angular readout can replace the sighting tube, but its mounting still needs an independently established level and angular zero.
The corrected instrument reads apparent altitude, including atmospheric refraction. Under ordinary conditions atmospheric refraction raises a low direction, so if R is the upward angular correction, γapp​=γgeom​+R. Subtracting the instrument zero does not subtract R. Record site height, temperature and pressure if applying a refraction model: these are explicit observer inputs in the US Naval Observatory's NOVAS software. A coarse inclinometer may be unable to resolve the correction, and a local weather reading alone does not determine every atmospheric layer. [ref].

At the zenith, every value of azimuth produces (E,N,U)=(0,0,1). There is no horizontal component to identify a bearing: atan2(0,0) cannot provide a geometrically meaningful azimuth, even if software returns a number. This coordinate singularity is a defect of the angular description; the viewing direction itself remains regular. The same ambiguity occurs at the opposite downward vertical. Near the zenith, two directions at fixed altitude separated by a small azimuth increment dη have separation cosγ∣dη∣ to first order, with angles in radians. At altitude 89∘, a 1∘ azimuth increment spans only about 0.01745∘ on that small arc. An optical telescope can consequently require a large bearing change for a small change of pointing near the zenith; working with unit vectors avoids inventing a preferred bearing at the singular point.

Horizontal coordinate system OurBigBook.com
The astronomical horizon is the great circle where the horizontal plane through the observer intersects the celestial sphere. It is perpendicular to the local vertical, so every direction on the astronomical horizon has altitude 0∘ and zenith distance 90∘. In the local horizontal coordinate system, it consists of the unit vectors satisfying n⋅eU​=0. This geometric reference remains defined when buildings or mountains hide it; a visible skyline is not a calibration of zero altitude.
Three boundaries must be distinguished. The astronomical horizon fixes the angular reference. Terrain supplies a site-dependent boundary with apparent altitude t(η) that changes with azimuth. Atmospheric refraction changes the apparent direction of incoming light, and can also change the apparent distant boundary. A point source clears an opaque terrain boundary only if γapp​>t(η) when both are expressed in the same apparent horizontal coordinate system; this clearance condition does not guarantee visibility through clouds or bright sky. In the synthetic diagram, a source with geometric altitude 3∘ and an imposed illustrative upward correction R=0.2∘ remains behind a 4∘ boundary. The chosen R is an algebraic illustration, not a fitted atmospheric prediction.
Even an unobstructed sea boundary need not coincide with the astronomical horizon. On a spherical Earth of radius r, an observer at height q sees the unrefracted tangent to the surface at a downward angle D satisfying cosD=r/(r+q). The right-angle tangent triangle supplies this relation; the visible boundary then has altitude −D. With illustrative r=6371km and q=10m, D≃0.1015∘, before atmospheric refraction. Raising the eye therefore changes the visible boundary without redefining the horizontal plane.
The US Naval Observatory's rise/set definitions explicitly distinguish the geometric reference from apparent contact with a visible disk: the standard Sun calculation puts its centre 50′ below the horizontal plane, combining an average 16′ radius with 34′ of atmospheric refraction. An equatorial coordinate system labels a viewing direction on the celestial sphere by right ascension α, increasing eastward around the reference celestial equator, and declination δ, increasing northward from that celestial equator. These two angles locate a direction, without specifying the object's Euclidean distance. In the traditional convention, zero right ascension points toward the reference equinox, the northward crossing of the Sun's annual path through the celestial equator. An hour circle through the direction supplies the north-south arc on which declination is measured. [ref].
For a concrete construction, choose Cartesian coordinates with x pointing toward the reference equinox, z toward the north reference celestial pole, and positive y given by the cross product of the positive z and x directions. The direction's unit vector is
n=(cosδcosα, cosδsinα, sinδ).
(12)
This is a spherical coordinate system with polar angle π/2−δ and no radial coordinate. The trigonometric functions require consistent angular units: convert right ascension in hours to radians before evaluating them. The synthetic direction α=4h=60∘, δ=30∘ gives n=(3​/4,3/4,1/2); its squared norm is 3/16+9/16+1/4=1. A change of reference axes applies a rotation to this unit vector before recovering the two angles. Away from the celestial poles, recover right ascension using the quadrant-aware atan2(ny​,nx​) reduced modulo 2π, and declination using arcsinnz​; a plain arctangent of ny​/nx​ loses the quadrant. Adding a common offset to every right ascension describes only the special case of a rotation about the same polar axis.
The reference specification matters. For an equatorial coordinate system tied to the Earth, precession changes the reference celestial equator and reference equinox, and nutation distinguishes their mean and true versions. The date specifying those axes is distinct from the astronomical epoch at which a catalogue's source directions apply: advancing a star's proper motion and changing reference axes are separate operations. A modern catalogue may instead use fixed reference frame axes, aligned approximately with the traditional J2000.0 axes, without a moving reference equinox. Thus a pair of numbers labelled merely "J2000" does not settle every convention. State the reference frame, the astronomical epoch, and whether a direction is catalogued or apparent. [ref].
During one night's elementary fixed-direction approximation, a star's right ascension and declination remain constant while its altitude, azimuth and hour angle change because the Earth turns. In angular units, with Θ the local sidereal time, west-positive hour angle H obeys
H=Θ−α(mod2π).
(13)
At upper meridian transit, H=0 and the local sidereal time equals the transiting direction's right ascension. Pair apparent sidereal time with apparent right ascension referred to the true celestial equator and reference equinox of date; mean sidereal time refers to the mean reference equinox. Raw fixed-frame catalogue coordinates require conversion before precision pointing. [ref].
This separation makes the equatorial coordinate system useful: a catalogue can identify a target independently of the observer's current astronomical horizon, while local sidereal time tells the observer which hour circle is on the celestial meridian. Precision observations also account for proper motion, stellar parallax, aberration of light and atmospheric refraction; the fixed-direction construction above omits those effects. A reference-axis rotation preserves angles between directions, whereas changing the observer or correcting atmospheric refraction is a different operation. [ref].

Equatorial coordinate system OurBigBook.com
Right ascension α is the eastward angle along the reference celestial equator from the reference equinox to a direction's hour circle, conventionally reduced to 0≤α<24h. Its hours label angles: 24h=360∘, 1h=15∘, 1m=15′ and 1s=15′′. Thus 6h30m=97.5∘=13π/24 radians. A minute of right ascension differs from a minute of arc, and the actual arc on a fixed-declination parallel also contains the cosine factor described under declination.
The hours become useful through sidereal time. At local sidereal time 8h, a synthetic direction of right ascension 6h30m has west-positive hour angle 1h30m=22.5∘ and has passed its upper meridian transit. Conversely, at 5h30m it has hour angle −1h and has yet to cross. Interpret these intervals in sidereal hours; ordinary civil hours are not interchangeable with them. The right ascension of the upper celestial meridian advances as the Earth turns, while the synthetic fixed target's right ascension stays unchanged.
An instrument makes this geometry tangible. DePauw University's description of McKim Observatory documents a meridian optical telescope with an angular circle, astronomical clocks and a chronograph. The circle measures zenith distance, and the crossing time supplies right ascension. Clock pulses and the observer's electrical key mark a rotating paper record, so crossing time is read relative to the clock marks. One clock kept sidereal time and another solar time. This apparatus separates two measured quantities: when a star crosses the celestial meridian, and at what angle from the zenith. [ref].
A teaching reconstruction would fix an optical telescope to sweep the celestial meridian, align its central sighting line, and observe a recognizable reference star followed by a target. Record each central-line crossing against a clock or timestamped camera, and read the angular circle at upper meridian transit. A short sequence shows the image moving across the stationary sighting line; the central crossing supplies a repeatable event. In the ideal model, successive upper crossings of a fixed direction recur once per sidereal day, and directions with increasing right ascension cross later in the same cycle. These are predictions for the reconstruction, rather than reported McKim measurements. Tatum derives the equality between local sidereal time and right ascension at upper meridian transit. [ref].
Calibrate the clock's zero by comparing its reference crossing readout Cr​ with the reference star's predicted apparent right ascension αr​ in the same date convention: the additive correction is b=αr​−Cr​, modulo 24h. Then infer target right ascension αt​=Ct​+b if the clock rate is correct between crossings. In a purely synthetic example, αr​=6h00m00s and Cr​=6h00m20s imply b=−20s. A target readout Ct​=6h30m20s therefore gives αt​=6h30m00s=97.5∘. The 20s clock offset is 300′′ in right ascension, while its local east-west angular effect at declination 60∘ is approximately 150′′. The reference and target in this calculation are invented directions, with no claim about any current star's coordinates.
Controls give the inference its meaning. Use independently established geographical latitude and an angular-circle zero for declination; check sighting-line alignment against several reference stars, and bracket the target in time with references to reveal clock drift. Record north or south of the zenith, distinguish upper from lower meridian transit, and account for atmospheric refraction. Convert the observing timestamp to local sidereal time using the site's east-positive longitude correction, rather than a time-zone offset; precise conversion uses the Earth's measured rotation time. A reference star calibrates a zero only after its catalogue direction has been converted to the observation convention. Repeated crossings reduce random measurement error, while an incorrect clock rate, axis alignment or catalogue convention remains a systematic limitation. [ref]. These controls are requirements inferred from the geometric and clock model, not a claimed historical observing log.

The observer's celestial meridian is the particular hour circle through the zenith. [ref].

A meridian transit is a direction's crossing of the observer's celestial meridian. Upper meridian transit occurs at hour angle 0 and gives the greatest geometric altitude in the fixed-direction model; lower meridian transit occurs at hour angle 12h and gives the least. Either crossing can lie below the astronomical horizon. [ref].

Light curve

Words: 1k Articles: 3
Astrophysics OurBigBook.com
A light curve records an astronomical source's received brightness against time, in a specified photometric passband. Its measured form is a time series of timestamps, brightness estimates, and uncertainties; a smooth F(t) is a model of that record. Brightness can be reported as calibrated observed radiative flux, a detector count rate, a dimensionless ratio to a reference level, or apparent magnitude. These quantities require different units and calibration conventions. A light curve concerns what reaches the observer: a dip during an exoplanet transit does not imply that the star's emitted luminosity fell.
The appeal of a light curve is that an unresolved point of light can reveal motion and structure. In exoplanet transit photometry, repeated dips constrain the orbital period; under the uniform-disc, dark-planet, full-overlap assumptions, the exoplanet transit depth is the blocked area fraction (Rp​/R⋆​)2. A toy one-percent dip therefore corresponds to a radius ratio of 0.10. Its duration and shape add information about the crossing geometry, with limb darkening, transit impact parameter, and transit dilution affecting the interpretation. See exoplanet transit photometry for the geometry. The first figure instead follows the measurement: an instrumental trend and sky contribution can obscure a small physical dip.
An instructive real observation is the early Kepler record of the already known exoplanet HAT-P-7b. Welsh and colleagues analysed 33.5 days from 13 May to 15 June 2009, containing 15 complete exoplanet transits at an orbital period of about 2.20473 days. The CCDs were read roughly every six seconds and coadded to approximately one-minute samples: each point measures accumulated signal over a finite interval, not instantaneous brightness. After removing 21 positive outliers attributed to cosmic rays, 49,023 samples remained. The authors estimated a scatter of about 150 parts per million per one-minute sample. A gradual 0.13% count decrease, suspected to arise from focus drift with a fixed extraction aperture, was removed with a cubic polynomial fitted while masking the exoplanet transits. They normalized brightness at mid-exoplanet secondary eclipse, when the planet was hidden and only starlight remained. [ref].
What does the instrument actually measure? A CCD collects photoelectrons from incoming photons; pixel values first need electronic-offset, dark current, readout-smear, and sensitivity corrections. [ref]. Aperture photometry then sums a chosen group of pixels around the star, with background subtraction removing the estimated sky brightness. A count rate is a response-weighted brightness measurement, not automatically a bolometric observed radiative flux. Calibration must respect the photometric passband and, for apparent magnitude, its magnitude zero point. Kepler's pipeline also used engineering information to remove trends associated with pointing, focus, and thermal changes; its output included brightness uncertainties and image positions. [ref].
Calibration and interpretation need separate checks. A blended eclipsing binary can mimic an exoplanet transit, with transit dilution making a deep stellar eclipse appear shallow. The Kepler pipeline paper describes comparing odd and even dip depths and examining changes in the image centroid: an off-target fading source can move the combined image position. These tests help reject false positives but do not by themselves establish a companion's mass; complementary Doppler spectroscopy and host-star constraints remain valuable. [ref].
Even a real exoplanet's signal can have several contributors. Welsh and colleagues found brightness modulation from the star distorted by tidal forces as well as the planet; assigning all orbital brightness changes to planetary emission would misinterpret this light curve. [ref]. Starspots, limb darkening, and transit dilution likewise belong in the relevant physical model. A flexible trend fitted through a dip could absorb that dip; the masked fit in the real example illustrates why the fitting procedure is part of the measurement. Exposure-averaged light curves and phase folding of a light curve make two further limitations explicit.

Aperture photometry (r=(S−nb)/Δt)

Words: 248
Light curve OurBigBook.com
Aperture photometry estimates brightness by summing calibrated detector pixels in an extraction region and subtracting the estimated background in that region. For n equally weighted pixels, let S be their total accumulated signal in electrons, b the estimated background electrons per pixel over the same exposure, and Δt the exposure duration. Then r=(S−nb)/Δt is a background-subtracted electron rate. Kepler applied aperture photometry to calibrated pixels with a fitted sky background. [ref].
This measurement trades source collection against background: enlarging the extraction region can retain more starlight but includes more sky brightness and neighbouring sources. Photon shot noise, read noise, and uncertainty in background subtraction contribute to its uncertainty. Dividing r by a consistently measured reference rate gives a dimensionless light curve; it does not supply an absolute observed radiative flux. If contaminating light remains, the reference includes it and the inferred exoplanet transit depth suffers transit dilution.
In the first toy figure, the source's reference rate is 100,000 electrons per second, the summed sky contribution is 4,000 electrons per second, and a known multiplicative response is g(t)=1+0.0003t with t in hours from mid-transit. The artificial exoplanet transit depth is 0.010, its total duration four hours, and its flat-bottom duration 2.8 hours; the straight ingress and egress are a toy approximation, not an exact exoplanet transit photometry model. Each synthetic sample averages a 0.5-hour exposure and adds seeded normal distribution noise with relative standard deviation 0.0006. Subtracting the known sky rate and dividing by the known response and reference rate recovers the dip. Real observations require estimating those corrections and carrying their uncertainty.

Exposure-averaged light curve (Fi​)

Words: 194
Light curve OurBigBook.com
An exposure-averaged light curve models what a finite exposure measures. For a constant response during an exposure of duration Δti​>0, centred at ti​, the expected mean brightness is
Fi​=Δti​1​∫ti​−Δti​/2ti​+Δti​/2​F(t)dt.
(15)
The integral has units of brightness times time; division restores the units of F. Observed points fluctuate around this mean. A response that changes during the exposure must instead be included inside the integral, as in the first figure's known drift. Exposure duration and the interval between samples are distinct: there may be dead time or missing exposures.
A short dip can be blurred even with perfectly noiseless measurements. For a toy rectangular dip of fractional depth δ and duration T<Δt, an exposure containing the whole dip has fractional depth δT/Δt: averaging hides part of its depth. A 1% dip lasting ten minutes therefore appears only 0.333% deep in a thirty-minute exposure. No interpolation recovers its shape from that single number without additional assumptions. Forward modelling should average the predicted light curve over each exposure before comparing it with the measurements. Kipping's analysis of exoplanet transit photometry demonstrates how ignoring this averaging biases inferred system parameters. [ref].

Phase folding of a light curve (ϕi​)

Words: 425
Light curve OurBigBook.com
Phase folding of a light curve maps timestamps onto a trial cycle of duration P>0. Given a reference time t0​, define the phase in cycles by
ϕi​=frac(Pti​−t0​​),0≤ϕi​<1,
(16)
where frac(x)=x−⌊x⌋ is the fractional part, using the floor function also for negative x. Plot brightness against ϕi​ rather than ti​; measurements separated by an integer multiple of P occupy the same phase. For a periodic function F(t+P)=F(t), this reveals the shared shape of many cycles. Folding changes coordinates; it neither averages samples nor chooses the correct P by itself. Welsh et al.'s folded Kepler plot separates the exoplanet transit and orbital brightness modulation. [ref].
The second figure uses a completely synthetic trapezoidal dip: P=3 days, t0​=1 day, and the same 1% depth and four-hour duration as the first figure. Different colours identify four successive cycles. Correct folding superimposes the dips; a wrong trial orbital period spreads them out. If P′=P+ϵ, the centre of the nth repeated event shifts by approximately −nϵ/P cycles when folded on P′, for ∣ϵ∣≪P. With P′=3.03 days, the fourth plotted event is displaced by −3(0.03)/3.03≃−0.0297 cycles. Transit-timing variations can also smear a constant-period fold, so retain the original timestamps and inspect individual events.
One may combine nearby phases with a weighted mean, but the uncertainty reduction requires assumptions. For N independent measurements with common standard deviation σ and effectively the same expected brightness within the bin, their arithmetic mean has standard deviation σ/N​. Thus sixteen independent 0.0006-precision samples give 0.00015 precision on that phase-bin mean. Shared calibration errors, changing starspots, and bins wide enough to mix ingress with out-of-transit brightness violate these assumptions. A folded plot can conceal changes between cycles. Gaussian process models can represent correlated variability and interpolate irregular samples, but their predictions and uncertainties depend on their assumed covariance function.
The bottom panels show the same model as relative brightness f=F/F0​ and as magnitude difference in one fixed photometric passband with a fixed magnitude zero point:
Δm(t)=−2.5log10​f(t),f(t)>0.
(17)
A dip to f=0.99 gives Δm≃+0.010912 magnitudes: fainter means a larger apparent magnitude. The figure places larger magnitude differences lower on the page so the two dip shapes are easy to compare; reversing that plotting convention does not change the formula. For f=1−δ and small δ, expansion of the logarithm gives Δm≃(2.5/ln10)δ≃1.085736δ. The exact transform is nonlinear: transforming an exposure's mean brightness is generally different from averaging its instantaneous apparent magnitudes. The ordinary logarithm cannot be applied to a nonpositive background-subtracted measurement; keep such measurements and their uncertainties in brightness units for an appropriate statistical model.

Luminosity (L)

Words: 409 Articles: 8
Astrophysics OurBigBook.com
Luminosity is emitted radiative power: the energy carried away by electromagnetic radiation per unit time, measured in watts. Bolometric luminosity includes all wavelengths; a measurement through one photometric passband captures only part of it. Spectral luminosity records how that power is distributed over frequency. Received observed radiative flux has different units, watts per square metre, because it measures what crosses an observer's collecting area. [ref].
For example, an ideal source with luminosity 1026W emits 1026J each second regardless of whether it is viewed from 20 or 40 parsecs. Its observed radiative flux changes with distance, while its luminosity remains fixed. Combining stellar parallax with observed radiative flux therefore lets us compare the actual outputs of stars rather than their apparent brightnesses.

Astronomical magnitude

Words: 2k Articles: 21
Astrophysics OurBigBook.com
Astronomical magnitude expresses brightness on a logarithmic scale: equal steps in astronomical magnitude represent equal ratios of received radiative flux. The scale runs backwards, so a brighter source has a smaller astronomical magnitude. A difference of five magnitudes means exactly a factor of 100 in flux; one magnitude means a factor of 1001/5≃2.511886, rather than exactly 2.5. This compresses the enormous range of astronomical brightnesses into manageable numbers. [ref].
Apparent magnitude describes received brightness, while absolute magnitude compares sources at a shared reference distance. Both require a specified photometric passband and magnitude zero point. A magnitude difference turns a ratio of positive radiative fluxes into a difference of numbers; it does not measure an additive change in emitted luminosity.

Magnitude difference (Δm)

Astronomical magnitude OurBigBook.com
For two positive measurements F1​,F2​ in the same photometric passband, using the same magnitude zero point, units, and weighting convention, their apparent magnitudes obey
Δm=m2​−m1​=−2.5log10​(F1​F2​​),F1​F2​​=10−0.4Δm.
(18)
The logarithm takes a dimensionless ratio. An energy-weighted measurement must be compared with another energy-weighted measurement, and a photon-counting measurement with another consistently calibrated photon-counting measurement. Changing photometric passband or magnitude zero point requires the corresponding calibration, as in a colour index. [ref]. [ref].
For example, F2​=100F1​ gives Δm=−5: source 2 is brighter. Conversely, Δm=+5 gives F2​/F1​=0.01, and Δm=+1 gives F2​/F1​≃0.398107. Even fractional steps work: Δm=+0.1 gives F2​/F1​≃0.912011, an approximately 8.80% decrease. These are illustrative ratios, independent of any particular star catalogue.

Apparent magnitude (m)

Words: 333 Articles: 3
Astronomical magnitude OurBigBook.com
Apparent magnitude m is a calibrated description of the observed radiative flux received from an astronomical source. It answers how bright the source appears in a specified photometric passband, rather than how much luminosity the source emits. Define Fref​>0 as the measurement assigned zero apparent magnitude by the chosen magnitude zero point. Then
m=−2.5log10​(Fref​F​).
(19)
Here F is the positive passband measurement, with the same units and response convention as Fref​. For an energy-weighted detector this measures received radiative flux through its response; for a photon-counting detector use the corresponding calibrated count rate for both quantities. Actual photometric passbands include the instrument's response across wavelength, so naming the photometric system is part of reporting an apparent magnitude. [ref]. [ref].
As toy examples in one photometric passband, F=Fref​ gives m=0, F=100Fref​ gives m=−5, and F=0.01Fref​ gives m=+5. A negative apparent magnitude therefore means more received radiative flux than the reference; it is physically allowed. Zero apparent magnitude does not mean zero radiative flux. The ordinary logarithm formula requires F>0.
A small apparent magnitude alone cannot distinguish a nearby faint source from a distant source with large luminosity: this is the flux-distance degeneracy. Stellar parallax supplies independent distance information, while a calibrated standard candle supplies intrinsic brightness. Interstellar extinction also changes the received radiative flux and hence the measured apparent magnitude.

The traditional near- and thermal-infrared photometric bands in the 1–5 micrometre region are J,H,K,L,M, with approximate centers 1.25,1.65,2.2,3.5,4.8 micrometres. Variants such as Ks​, L′ and M′ have different detailed responses. They largely follow atmospheric windows; transmission, sky brightness, and detector response determine practical band edges. Absolute magnitude (M)

Words: 572 Articles: 8
Astronomical magnitude OurBigBook.com
Absolute magnitude M, in the stellar convention used here, is the apparent magnitude a source would have at 10 parsecs, with interstellar extinction removed. The hypothetical observation uses the specified photometric passband and magnitude zero point, preserving the source's emitted spectrum and luminosity. Moving every source to this common distance lets us compare intrinsic brightness without confusing it with distance. [ref].
For a fixed source with isotropy of emission, in transparent space with negligible relativistic and cosmological effects, the inverse-square law gives the hypothetical measurement F10​ and absolute magnitude
F10​=F(d)(10pcd​)2,M=−2.5log10​(Fref​F10​​).
(20)
The factor applies in the same photometric passband, with unchanged emitted spectrum. Thus absolute magnitude compares luminosity in that response, rather than automatically the total bolometric luminosity over all wavelengths.
Consider a toy source with M=0. Its apparent magnitude is m=0 at 10 parsecs, m=5 at 100 parsecs, and m=10 at 1000 parsecs, neglecting interstellar extinction. Its absolute magnitude remains M=0 throughout: moving the observer changes received radiative flux, not emitted luminosity. Another toy source with M=−5 has 100 times its passband output under the same isotropy and calibration assumptions. Negative absolute magnitudes are allowed too; "absolute" names the reference-distance convention, not an absolute value.
A calibrated standard candle reverses this reasoning: its known absolute magnitude and measured apparent magnitude give a distance modulus. This is why estimating intrinsic brightness is so useful for measuring astronomical distances. [ref].

Finite-band corrections use the actual detector response and magnitude zero point.

Photon energy and arrival-rate redshifts supply two factors of 1+z, while the observed frequency interval is reduced by one. Substitution of the power-law spectrum gives the displayed K correction. A standard candle is an astronomical source whose calibrated absolute magnitude or luminosity allows its apparent magnitude or flux to determine a distance. A population with unknown common absolute magnitude only determines relative distances without an external luminosity calibration. Type Ia supernova cosmology models this distinction explicitly.

A standardizable candle has a predictable absolute magnitude after correcting measured source properties, rather than identical intrinsic brightness for every object. Type Ia supernova cosmology uses light curve shape and colour for this purpose.

Standard candle OurBigBook.com
A flux-limited sample preferentially includes intrinsically brighter objects at a given distance. Calibrating standard candles from that selected sample can bias inferred distances.

Malmquist bias OurBigBook.com
For a uniform Euclidean population, a complete flux-limited sample weights luminosity by accessible volume L3/2. Since L∝10−0.4M, an intrinsic Gaussian magnitude distribution is multiplied by e−0.6ln(10)M. Completing the square shifts its mean by the displayed amount without changing its variance. Extra distance bounds, extinction, evolution and other selection cuts alter this simple result.

Words: 57
Malmquist bias OurBigBook.com
A noise-free flux threshold truncates the distance distribution of objects with exactly identical relevant-band luminosity. It cannot preferentially select intrinsically brighter members when no luminosity scatter exists. A luminosity distribution introduces the accessible-volume weighting L3/2 in homogeneous Euclidean space. Measurement scatter across the flux threshold and nonuniform completeness introduce additional selection effects even for identical intrinsic luminosities.

Malmquist bias OurBigBook.com
For a flux threshold fmin​ and isotropic point-source luminosity L, the detection radius is rmax​=L/(4πfmin​)​. In a homogeneous Euclidean population the accessible volume is proportional to L3/2, so the selected luminosity distribution is proportional to φ(L)L3/2. This assumes flux selection and inverse-square propagation, not an arbitrary surface-brightness-selected diffuse field.

Astronomical magnitude OurBigBook.com
The distance modulus compares received brightness with intrinsic brightness through μ=m−M, the difference between apparent magnitude and absolute magnitude in the same photometric passband and magnitude zero point. With no interstellar extinction, fixed emitted spectrum and luminosity, isotropy of emission, and the local inverse-square law, it determines Euclidean distance:
μ=m−M=5log10​(10pcd​),d=10pc10μ/5.
(21)
The ratio inside the logarithm is dimensionless. To see the factor 5, use the inverse-square law in the magnitude difference formula:
F10​F(d)​=(d10pc​)2,m−M=−2.5log10​[(d10pc​)2].
(22)
For example, m=5 and M=0 give μ=5, hence d=10pc×10=100pc. A tenfold increase in distance adds five magnitudes; an increase of one magnitude multiplies distance by 101/5≃1.584893. The distance modulus is a logarithmic scale for distance, not a distance in length units. [ref].
At 10 parsecs, μ=0 and m=M. Within 10 parsecs, the distance modulus is negative; for example, μ=−5 gives the positive distance d=1pc. A negative distance modulus does not imply negative distance. At cosmological distances, the inference needs luminosity distance and a K correction; the simple local formula must not silently absorb these effects.
Interstellar extinction increases apparent magnitude. The observed distance modulus then includes both geometric dimming and attenuation; extinction bias in photometric distance explains how to separate them.

Extinction bias in photometric distance (dinferred​/d=10A/5)

Let A≥0 be the interstellar extinction in magnitudes in the specified photometric passband. Compared with the same unobscured source at the same distance, its radiative flux is multiplied by 10−0.4A, so its apparent magnitude increases by A. Consequently,
m−M=5log10​(10pcd​)+A,μ0​=m−M−A.
(23)
Here μ0​ is the extinction-corrected distance modulus. The correction subtracts A before using the distance formula. Caltech's NED distance-method documentation explicitly distinguishes an apparent distance modulus from an extinction-corrected distance modulus. [ref].
Ignoring positive interstellar extinction attributes too much dimming to distance, producing an overestimate:
ddinferred​​=10A/5.
(24)
As an illustrative toy, put the source with M=0 at 100 parsecs behind A=1 magnitude of interstellar extinction. The measured apparent magnitude is m=6. Setting A=0 incorrectly gives dinferred​=10pc×106/5≃158.489pc, a factor 1.584893 too large. Subtracting the known A=1 recovers 100 parsecs. The diagram's fixed A=1 offset is a controlled illustration, not a model of how actual interstellar extinction grows with distance, and none of its values are star catalogue measurements.

Ultraviolet catastrophe
Words: 104
Rayleigh-Jeans law OurBigBook.com
The ultraviolet catastrophe is the divergent total thermal radiation energy predicted by classical equipartition theorem applied to the electromagnetic mode density in a box. Each mode has mean energy kB​T, while the number of modes per volume per frequency is 8πν2/c3. The Rayleigh-Jeans law therefore gives uν​=8πkB​Tν2/c3, whose integral over all positive frequencies diverges at every T>0.
Planck's law replaces the classical mode energy by hν/(ehν/(kB​T)−1). It agrees with equipartition when hν≪kB​T but suppresses high-frequency excitations exponentially. The resulting spectral energy density is integrable and yields the finite Stefan–Boltzmann law. The failure concerns the classical equilibrium distribution of energy among modes, not the existence of electromagnetic wave propagation itself.

Wien's displacement law

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Planck function OurBigBook.com
Wien's displacement law says that the wavelength maximizing the Planck function per unit wavelength, Bλ​(T), moves inversely with absolute temperature:
λmax​T=b,b≃2.897771955×10−3mK.
(28)
Here b is the Wien displacement constant. Heating an ideal blackbody therefore shifts this peak toward shorter wavelengths, while also increasing its emission at every fixed wavelength. The peak identifies where equal narrow wavelength intervals carry the most power; it is not a single emitted wavelength. Planck's law supplies the full curve, and the Stefan–Boltzmann law supplies its integral.
Specify the spectral coordinate before finding a peak. The frequency form of Wien's displacement law maximizes Bν​, which is spectral radiance per unit frequency. Its maximum is not c/λmax​. The frequency and wavelength spectral radiance conversion changes the density as well as the horizontal coordinate; the existing frequency and wavelength peaks of Planck's law give a complementary numerical comparison.
In his 11 December 1911 Nobel lecture, Wilhelm Wien explained the displacement principle through a thought experiment: compress black-body radiation between reflecting moving walls. Work against radiation pressure raises the energy density, while reflection changes each frequency by the Doppler effect. The Second law of thermodynamics connects the resulting spectrum to one at a higher temperature. This determines how the spectrum scales between temperatures, without determining its complete shape. The Wien approximation is a separate, restricted spectral formula.[ref]

Here h is the Planck constant, kB​ the Boltzmann constant, and c the speed of light. Since dx/dλ=−x/λ=0, an interior maximum in wavelength is also a stationary point in x. A logarithmic derivative gives

Thus g first increases and then decreases to negative values, crossing zero exactly once for x>0. Since x5/(ex−1) tends to zero at both endpoints, this stationary point is the unique global maximum. Solving the definition of x for wavelength gives

Now stipulate a photodetector with constant quantum efficiency η over the relevant wavelengths, collecting equal narrow wavelength bins. For fixed accepted projected area times solid angle G, with dilution included in G, its expected photon count rate density is

For example, G=10−12m2sr, η=0.5 and a 1nm bin centered at 0.600μm give approximately 1.93×1010 detected photons per second in the narrow-bin approximation. where Si,0​ is the background reading and Ri​ includes spectral selection, optical transmission and detector spectral responsivity. A raw channel maximum need not locate either Planck function maximum. Recovering a temperature requires an appropriate calibrated response and an emission model. Coblentz's cavity-radiation spectrum measurement
Words: 192
Wien's displacement law OurBigBook.com
William Weber Coblentz's primary report describes an electrically heated porcelain cavity wound with platinum ribbon. Mirrors imaged its central radiating diaphragm onto a 0.6mm optical slit; a fluorite optical prism dispersed the beam onto a vacuum bolometer. Galvanometer deflections read the detector response. A resistance standard checked electrical sensitivity, while repeated readings checked stability. Sodium lines fixed the angular zero; a refractive index curve supplied wavelengths and slit-bandwidth corrections. Thermocouples were standardized at freezing points of zinc, antimony and copper. Drying the optical path reduced atmospheric absorption; prism scattering and temperature calibration remained limitations. These were Coblentz's measurements. His extraction of radiation constants assumed the Planck law, so it was not a model-independent proof of the spectral formula.[ref]
The inference to test is whether corrected spectra taken at independently determined temperatures have their Bλ​ maxima at a constant product λmax​T. Comparing raw galvanometer deflections at different optical prism settings would also compare different wavelength widths and optical losses. The response integral in blackbody peak and detector response explains why those corrections belong to the physical inference rather than merely to presentation.

Radiative flux OurBigBook.com
For a steady point-like astronomical source with isotropy of emission, in transparent space with negligible relativistic or cosmological effects, conservation of energy spreads its luminosity over a sphere of surface area 4πd2. Its bolometric observed radiative flux is
F=4πd2L​,L=4πd2F.
(44)
This inverse-square law reflects geometric dilution: the same emitted power crosses increasingly large spheres. It does not require light to lose energy on the journey. For a fixed luminosity, doubling Euclidean distance quarters the observed radiative flux. [ref].
With L0​=1026W and d0​=20 parsecs, the result is F0​≃2.09×10−11Wm−2. At 40 parsecs, the same source gives F0​/4≃5.22×10−12Wm−2. An ideal collecting area of 1m2 at 20 parsecs intercepts approximately 2.09×10−11W, before detector losses.

Flux-distance degeneracy ((L,d)↦(k2L,kd))
Words: 92
Observed radiative flux OurBigBook.com
One observed radiative flux cannot determine both luminosity and Euclidean distance: for every k>0, replacing (L,d) by (k2L,kd) leaves F unchanged. In particular, 4×1026W at 40 parsecs produces the same observed radiative flux as 1026W at 20 parsecs. This is a concrete failure of identifiability in an inverse problem.
An independent stellar parallax fixes the distance and breaks this degeneracy; alternatively, a calibrated standard candle supplies the luminosity. Interstellar extinction can further reduce the observed radiative flux, and a photometric passband measures only a selected spectral range. At cosmological distances, use luminosity distance in the bolometric relation. Each inference must specify which radiative flux was measured and what propagation assumptions connect it to luminosity.

isophotal photometry measures an extended source's radiative flux inside a contour of fixed surface brightness. It misses light outside that contour. A per-pixel threshold is not a fundamental limit on fitting or averaging many faint pixels together.

X-ray astronomy

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Observational astronomy OurBigBook.com
X-ray astronomy infers the properties of celestial sources from their X-rays. It requires instruments above the strongly absorbing layers of Earth's terrestrial atmosphere. Riccardo Giacconi's 2002 Nobel lecture connects the early rocket detections to later grazing-incidence X-ray optics, which collect photons over a large entrance area onto a small detector.[ref]
The measurement is an inverse problem: a count rate mixes incident photon arrival rate, detector response, and background. A point-like astronomical source produces a direction-dependent excess as the instrument scans; diffuse X-ray background contributes over many directions. Neither a count excess nor a narrow feature by itself determines the emission mechanism. The useful progression is from detecting an excess, to locating it, to measuring its spectrum and light curve.

Cosmic X-ray source

X-ray astronomy OurBigBook.com

1962 rocket discovery of cosmic X-ray sources

Words: 316 Articles: 1
X-ray astronomy OurBigBook.com
In 1962, Riccardo Giacconi and colleagues flew three Geiger counters to search for lunar X-ray fluorescence. Different mica thicknesses tested penetration; lampblack blocked ultraviolet. Each counter sat in an anticoincidence detector using a scintillation counter to reject cosmic rays. There was no mechanical collimator. Rotation scanned the sky; optical sensors supplied orientation.[ref]
Counts were sorted by azimuth; a faulty counter and tumbling descent data were excluded. A directional peak lay above a diffuse component. Window, altitude and angular responses tested X-rays against charged particles; the Moon's nondetection checked optical leakage. The authors argued for an origin outside the Solar system, while residual cosmic ray background was not directly measured and source size, position and spectrum remained assumption-dependent.[ref]
A simple original forward problem makes the distinction precise. Let ϕ be the scan azimuth, let g(ϕ) be a dimensionless directional response with maximum one, let F be a source's band-integrated photon arrival rate per unit area, let A0​ be its on-axis X-ray effective area, and let b be a constant accepted background rate. The expected rate is
r(ϕ)=FA0​g(ϕ)+b.
(46)
For a broad illustrative response g(ϕ)=max(0,cosϕ), the full width at half maximum is 120∘: cosϕ=1/2 at ϕ=±60∘. For a one-dimensional ideal collimator model g(ϕ)=max(0,1−∣ϕ∣/θc​), the full width at half maximum is θc​. Choosing θc​=20∘ narrows the response sixfold without focusing any additional photons. These are teaching response functions, not reconstructions of the rocket's window transmission or geometry. A narrower scan peak can reflect the instrument response even when the source is unresolved.

Diffuse X-ray background

Words: 48
X-ray astronomy OurBigBook.com
Diffuse X-ray background is X-ray emission spread over the instrument's observed sky rather than assigned to a single resolved source. Diffuse appearance at finite angular resolution does not prove emission by a continuous medium: many unresolved point-like astronomical sources can also give a smooth signal. Instrumental background is a separate contribution, even though both enter measured counts.

X-ray effective area (Aeff​)

Words: 541 Articles: 1
X-ray astronomy OurBigBook.com
X-ray effective area is the area that converts an incident photon arrival rate per unit area into an accepted count rate. For a fixed direction and a sufficiently narrow energy interval, write
Aeff​=Ageom​Tηϵs​,Ns​=FAeff​t.
(47)
Here Ageom​ is projected geometric area, T is transmittance through windows or optics, η is quantum efficiency, ϵs​ is the probability that a detected source event passes event selection, and t is live observing time. Ns​ is an expected value, not a guarantee of an integer count. Multiplication follows by counting incident photons over area and time, then applying the successive conditional acceptance probabilities. Live time already excludes intervals when the instrument cannot record events; multiplying by a live-time fraction again would count the same loss twice.
For an invented narrow-band example, choose Ageom​=40cm2, T=0.8, η=0.75, and ϵs​=5/6. Then Aeff​=20cm2. A source with F=0.30photonscm−2s−1 observed for t=100s gives Ns​=600. F here counts photons; converting it into observed radiative flux requires their energies. If all have energy E0​, the corresponding radiative flux is E0​F.
A broad spectrum instead requires
Ns​=t∫FE​(E)Aeff​(E)dE,
(48)
where FE​ is the differential photon arrival rate per area and energy. A single band-averaged X-ray effective area depends on the assumed spectrum. This is why a count rate alone cannot give an assumption-free radiative flux.
On-off X-ray photon counting (S=Non​−αNoff​)
Words: 343
X-ray effective area OurBigBook.com
Background subtraction must account for uncertainty in the background measurement itself. In an original idealized experiment, an on-source exposure contains source and background, while an independent off-source exposure contains background alone. Assume stationary rates and identical background acceptance per unit live time. With α=ton​/toff​, let independent counts obey Poisson distributions:
Non​∼Poisson(S+B),Noff​∼Poisson(B/α).
(49)
Then linearity of expectation and addition of variances for independent random variables give
S=Non​−αNoff​,ES=S,Var(S)=S+(1+α)B.
(50)
The result concerns accepted source counts S, after all efficiencies. For large counts the normal approximation gives the descriptive signal-to-noise ratio in photon counting
Zapprox​=Non​+α2Noff​​S​.
(51)
This plug-in ratio is not an exact null-hypothesis significance. Small counts require the discrete Poisson model; searching many sky directions also changes a detection claim's p-value.
Choose ton​=100s and toff​=200s, with observed counts Non​=1000 and Noff​=800. Thus α=1/2, S=600, and the estimated standard deviation is 1200​=34.64 counts. The inferred F=S/(Aeff​ton​)=0.300±0.0173photonscm−2s−1 uses the preceding Aeff​=20cm2 and includes counting uncertainty only. The descriptive ratio is 17.32. Treating the scaled off-source background as exact would omit 200 counts squared from the estimated variance.
For a selection-design comparison, suppose before a veto the expected source contribution is S0​=750, the on-source background is B0​=2000, and α=1/2. Let source acceptance be ϵs​=0.8 and background acceptance be ϵb​=0.2. Then S=600, B=400, and S/S+(1+α)B​=17.32, whereas omitting the veto gives 750/750+3000​=12.25. Rejection helps because the background is reduced enough to compensate for lost source events. A different veto can make matters worse; source efficiency and background rejection are separate probabilities. This comparison is an independent teaching example, not the efficiency calibration used above.
If both exposure times grow with fixed α and stationary rates, S=ston​ and B=bton​ imply Z≃ston​​/s+(1+α)b​. Four times the live time doubles this ideal ratio. Misestimated background rates, uncertain X-ray effective area, and source variability can defeat that scaling; longer exposure does not remove systematic error.

Grazing-incidence X-ray optics

Words: 261
X-ray astronomy OurBigBook.com
Grazing-incidence X-ray optics redirect X-rays by shallow specular reflections along mirror surfaces. Riccardo Giacconi's lecture describes coaxial paraboloidal and hyperboloidal mirrors using two reflections, and the later Einstein observatory's imaging capability. Focusing separates collecting area from detector area: the collected source signal can remain large while the detector background is drawn from a smaller region.[ref]
An ideal lossless geometrical optics calculation explains the shallow angle. Take vacuum refractive index one and a material with real refractive index n=1−δ, where 0<δ≪1. Let θ be the grazing angle measured from the surface. Snell's law written for angles from the normal requires cosθ=nsinθt​. A propagating transmitted ray exists only if cosθ≤n. Thus the ideal threshold is
θc​=arccos(1−δ)≃2δ​.
(52)
The last step uses the Taylor series cosθ=1−θ2/2+O(θ4). For a chosen δ=2×10−5, θc​≃0.006325 radians, or 0.3624∘. Absorption makes the refractive index complex and softens this ideal threshold; surface roughness and alignment errors also reduce throughput or worsen the point spread function. These are reasons to calibrate X-ray effective area and angular resolution, rather than assume that reflection is perfect.
The benefit can be quantified without specifying a historical telescope. Suppose a source retains fraction f of its counts inside an extraction region, while a uniform detector background contributes qat counts over detector area a. In the background-dominated limit of the same independent on-off model,
Z≃(1+α)qa​fFAeff​t​​.
(53)
Reducing a by a factor of 100 at fixed f and X-ray effective area improves this ideal ratio tenfold. A collimator restricts admitted directions; focusing optics bring selected rays together. An image also separates nearby sources and identifies clean background regions, connecting optical design directly to a better constrained inverse problem.

Observational astronomy OurBigBook.com
Radio astronomy studies celestial sources through their radio waves. The long wavelengths make angular resolution expensive: a filled telescope of diameter D has a characteristic diffraction scale of order λ/D. Aperture synthesis instead combines measurements from separated antennas, using their separations to measure fine structure while their individual collecting areas determine how much radiation they receive. A kilometre-wide arrangement of small antennas does not collect the power intercepted by a filled kilometre-wide dish.

The equivalent input noise temperature of the antenna-plus-receiver system is defined by available noise power Pn​=kB​Tsys​Δν in one matched polarization of waves mode. It includes receiver noise and the appropriate sky and instrumental contributions. It is not generally the physical temperature of a single component.
