System temperature OurBigBook.com
The system-equivalent flux density is the unpolarized spectral flux density that would produce an antenna temperature equal to Tsys​. With effective collecting area Ae​, SEFD=2kB​Tsys​/Ae​. The factor two follows from one polarization of waves measurement of an unpolarized source. State effective area and polarization of waves conventions when comparing sensitivities.[ref]

A radio telescope is an astronomical instrument that receives radio waves using an antenna and associated receivers. A single dish measures radiation over its directional sensitivity pattern; separated elements can supply complex visibilities for aperture synthesis.

Interplanetary scintillation

Words: 48
Radio astronomy OurBigBook.com
Interplanetary scintillation is rapid variation in the received strength of a compact astronomical radio source, produced by propagation through fluctuating electron density in the solar wind. Its dependence on source angular size can help distinguish compact sources. It is a propagation effect, distinct from intrinsic periodic emission by a pulsar.

Aperture synthesis

Words: 2k Articles: 25
Radio astronomy OurBigBook.com
Aperture synthesis reconstructs the sky's brightness from complex visibilities measured at different interferometric baselines. Each measurement constrains a Fourier transform component of the brightness, rather than supplying a little photograph. Combining many such components can distinguish sources that each individual antenna leaves unresolved. The remarkable economy is that changing separations and the rotation of Earth can provide many measurements with only a few physical antennas.
Martin Ryle's Cambridge group made aperture synthesis a practical method of astronomical imaging at the Mullard Radio Astronomy Observatory. Cambridge's institutional history connects that work with the One-Mile Telescope and its larger successors.[ref]
In his 1974 lecture Radio Telescopes of Large Resolving Power, Martin Ryle recalled the problem of distinguishing weak extragalactic sources and resolving their structure. He explained sequential wavefront sampling using one simultaneously observed element as a wave phase reference, and the saving obtained by letting Earth rotate the apparent baseline.[ref]
The 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics distinguished Martin Ryle's observations and inventions, especially aperture synthesis, from Antony Hewish's role in discovering pulsars. The latter is a separate astronomical discovery, with its own observational history.[ref]
Synthesized beam (θsyn​∼λ/bmax​)
Words: 45
Aperture synthesis OurBigBook.com
The synthesized beam is the angular response produced by the sampled and weighted complex visibilities. Its characteristic width is set by the longest well-weighted projected interferometric baselines, of order λ/bmax​, while sidelobes reflect incomplete Fourier coverage. It differs from the individual antenna primary beam, which limits the field of view.
Radio interferometry
Words: 2k Articles: 19
Aperture synthesis OurBigBook.com
Radio interferometry measures the spatial coherence of received radio waves. At two antennas, a receiver preserves the relative wave phase, compensates the geometric delay for a chosen phase centre, and averages a product of one signal with the complex conjugate of the other. In a complex-signal description this correlation is ⟨E1​E2∗​⟩. Its real and imaginary parts carry two complementary components of the complex visibility; measuring only the received powers discards the relative wave phase needed for general imaging.
A finite frequency band makes delay compensation essential. If the residual delay is Δτ, the residual wave phase varies by 2πΔνΔτ across a band of width Δν. Averaging these differently oriented complex contributions reduces the correlation. For an ideal rectangular band the multiplicative factor is sin(πΔνΔτ)/(πΔνΔτ). A phase correction at just the central frequency cannot remove this variation across the band. Long time averages can likewise smear a changing signal.
Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA)
Words: 43
Radio interferometry OurBigBook.com
The Very Long Baseline Array is a radio-telescope array used for very-long-baseline interferometry. In a solar-deflection experiment, differential astrometry of nearby compact sources compares their apparent directions as their angular separation from the Sun changes. Measurements at several frequencies can distinguish dispersive refraction in the solar corona from achromatic gravitational deflection.[ref]

Words: 35
Radio interferometry OurBigBook.com
very-long-baseline interferometry correlates accurately time-referenced radio signals recorded at widely separated collectors, giving angular resolution of order wavelength divided by projected baseline. Geometric delays, frequency standards, atmospheric propagation and source structure enter the calibration. Compact maser positions and motions are one application.

Radio interferometry OurBigBook.com
A residual delay δτ in a rectangular band of width Δν attenuates the correlated amplitude by sinc(πΔνδτ). Coarse delay quantization must keep this factor near one; the relevant path scale is c/Δν. Separately, an untracked carrier phase has error 2πδℓ/λ. Fine phase rotation can remove that central-frequency phase while leaving the band-dependent decorrelation, so delay-step specifications must state both bandwidth and compensation architecture.

Radio interferometry OurBigBook.com
Independent visibility samples are combined with weights proportional to inverse noise variance. This maximizes the point-source sensitivity for correctly calibrated samples. Dense regions of the sampled Fourier plane receive more total weight; tapering the long baselines can further emphasize extended structure at the cost of angular resolution. A source-template filter instead also weights by predicted source response.

Radio interferometry OurBigBook.com
For N equal antennas, weak-source independent receiver noise, natural weighting and total on-source time t, the point-source rms in one polarization of waves is the displayed value. There are N(N−1)/2 independent cross-correlation baselines, each with real-component error SEFD/2Δνt​. Combining npol​ independent polarization of waves estimates reduces the rms by npol​​. Correlation losses divide the sensitivity by an efficiency factor; weighting, flagging and an extended source change the effective sensitivity.[ref]

The phase centre is the reference sky direction for removing geometric delay and its associated wave phase. An unresolved source exactly there ideally has constant complex visibility after calibration; a displaced source has a baseline-dependent wave phase.

An interferometric baseline is the displacement b=r2​−r1​ between two antennas. For a unit line of sight s0​ toward the phase centre, its projection onto the plane of the sky is

(54)
Here c is the speed of light. The signed delay depends on which receiver is delayed; the geometric path difference's magnitude does not. If eθ​ is a unit tangent in the direction being imaged, the dimensionless coordinate u=b⋅eθ​/λ is a spatial frequency, measured in cycles per radian of small sky offset. A single pair gives fringes of angular period 1/∣u∣ along that tangent. This period specifies one measured oscillation; it does not specify a whole image's angular resolution or eliminate ambiguous source arrangements.
The left panel separates the component producing the reference delay from the component measuring angular structure. The right panel shows a possible Earth-rotation aperture synthesis track, with its opposite complex conjugate track. Those opposite samples provide the symmetry required by a real brightness distribution; they are not independent extra observations.

The number of antennas alone does not fix either limiting baseline or supply zero-spacing total power.

The difference in plane-wave propagation time between two antennas is the projected baseline along the source direction divided by the speed of light. Its sign depends on the ordering of the receivers. A monochromatic signal acquires relative phase 2πντg​; its change with Earth rotation is compensated by fringe stopping for the chosen reference direction.
Residual phase of a tracked east-west interferometer (δϕ≃2πbαcosθ/λ)
Words: 49
Geometric delay OurBigBook.com
For an east-west baseline b and phase-centre zenith angle θ in its vertical plane, path compensation subtracts bsinθ. An offset α leaves δℓ=b[sin(θ+α)−sinθ]≃bαcosθ. The complex correlation therefore has phase 2πbαcosθ/λ, up to receiver-order convention. Equal cable lengths do not remove this sky-dependent path difference.
Earth-rotation aperture synthesis
Words: 147
Interferometric baseline OurBigBook.com
Earth-rotation aperture synthesis uses Earth's changing orientation to vary a fixed ground baseline's projection onto the plane of the sky. In two dimensions, u and v are the components of b⊥​/λ along two perpendicular sky tangents. Tracking one field traces a curve in this (u,v) plane; changing the physical baseline supplies other curves. A track samples Fourier transform coordinates, rather than the brightness along a track across the sky.
For a horizontal east–west baseline of length B, choose the sky-axis signs so that
u=λB​cosH,v=λB​sinδsinH,
(55)
where H is hour angle and δ is declination. The ellipse follows by projecting the rotating baseline onto sky tangents. At a celestial pole it is a circle; near the celestial equator its minor axis collapses. Thus the same ground layout constrains different sky directions unequally. Rotation improves coverage, but does not fill every spatial frequency, and synthesis across many hours assumes that the source changes negligibly during that interval.
Radio interferometer calibration
Words: 114
Radio interferometry OurBigBook.com
Radio interferometer calibration estimates instrumental and propagation effects that alter a complex visibility. A simple narrow-field model is
V12obs​=g1​g2∗​V12sky​+n12​,
(56)
where g1​,g2​ are complex receiver gains and n12​ represents additive noise. A point-like astronomical source of known position and stable strength constrains these gains: its expected complex visibility has a known wave phase and amplitude. A resolved or variable reference source requires a better source model. Errors in the reference model can be transferred into the inferred sky.
In a proposed extension, Martin Ryle described simultaneous observation of a nearby reference point source to correct atmospheric wave phase errors, using an additional dish at each element. He presented this as a possible extension, rather than the standard One-Mile Telescope arrangement.[ref]
Complex visibility (V(u,v))
Words: 570 Articles: 6
Radio interferometry OurBigBook.com
A complex visibility is a calibrated complex correlation of the signals received at a particular interferometric baseline. In a narrow field, with scalar radiation, the far-field approximation for an outgoing source, a narrow frequency channel, negligible noncoplanar phase curvature and a steady sky of mutually incoherent emitters,
V(u,v)=∬A(l,m)I(l,m)e−2πi(ul+vm)dldm.
(57)
Here l,m are small dimensionless sky-direction offsets, I is brightness in the chosen channel, and A is the primary beam. This is the Fourier transform of beam-weighted brightness. The two-dimensional formula requires those approximations: a wide field generally needs the third baseline coordinate and curved sky geometry.
For an explicit one-dimensional derivation, set the primary beam to one over the small field, and place independent emitters at angular offsets θj​. Choose a wave phase convention in which, after removing the phase centre's delay, their received complex amplitudes are
E1​(t)=∑j​aj​(t),E2​(t)=∑j​aj​(t)e2πiuθj​,⟨aj​ak∗​⟩=Ij​δjk​.
(58)
Here δjk​ is the Kronecker delta and angle brackets denote an expected value estimated by time averaging a steady signal. The last equality states mutual incoherence: different emitters have zero averaged cross term, although each emitter's two received copies remain correlated. Multiplying and averaging gives
V(u)=⟨E1​E2∗​⟩=∑j,k​⟨aj​ak∗​⟩e−2πiuθk​=∑j​Ij​e−2πiuθj​.
(59)
For continuous brightness this becomes V(u)=∫I(θ)e−2πiuθdθ. Real brightness implies the Hermitian symmetry V(−u)=V(u)∗; it does not require brightness to be even. In particular, an asymmetric real source usually has a nonzero imaginary complex visibility. At zero baseline, V(0)=∑j​Ij​ is the total beam-weighted source strength. Ordinary separated-element correlations need not measure that zero-baseline value.
Visibility of a one-dimensional uniform source (V/V(0)=sinc(πbp​Δα/λ))
Words: 57
Complex visibility OurBigBook.com
A centred uniform source of angular width Δα has normalized visibility V/V(0)=sinc(πbp​Δα/λ), with bp​ the projected baseline along that angular coordinate and sincx=sinx/x. The result is the integral of the point-source complex phase over source brightness. Its first null occurs at width λ/∣bp​∣; negative values are phase reversals rather than negative brightness.
Visibility of a uniform rectangular source (V=Sν​sinc(πΘx​u)sinc(πΘy​v))
Words: 62
Complex visibility OurBigBook.com
With constant surface brightness over a centred angular rectangle of widths Θx​,Θy​, and a nearly uniform primary beam over that rectangle, the Fourier transform separates into two one-dimensional integrals. The result is V(u,v)=Sν​sinc(πΘx​u)sinc(πΘy​v), where sincx=sinx/x. The zero-spacing value is the integrated spectral flux density, while the first axial null is at ∣u∣=1/Θx​. Long baselines therefore do not measure the total flux of a resolved rectangle.
Fringe stopping (Vstop​=Ve−iϕref​)
Words: 162 Articles: 2
Complex visibility OurBigBook.com
Electronic compensation of the time-dependent reference geometric delay multiplies each complex visibility by an opposite reference phase. A stationary point source at the phase centre then has constant corrected phase despite Earth rotation. antenna pointing alone does not perform this correction. Off-axis sources retain the relative fringe evolution that encodes their angular offsets.
Field-dependent averaging losses in radio interferometry (δνBθ/c≪1,ΔtΩE​Bθ/λ≪1)
Words: 118 Articles: 1
Fringe stopping OurBigBook.com
After delay tracking and fringe stopping at a phase center, an off-axis direction retains delay of order Bθ/c and rotation-induced fringe-rate offset of order ΩE​Bθ/λ. Averaging across a wide channel or long integration then decorrelates that direction. The displayed inequalities give order-of-magnitude small-smearing conditions; exact coefficients depend on baseline geometry, averaging window and allowed loss. A larger field or longer baseline therefore demands finer frequency and time sampling.
Bandwidth decorrelation of a point source (Vavg​=V(ν0​)sinc(πΔντ))
Words: 49
Field-dependent averaging losses in radio interferometry OurBigBook.com
A point source away from the tracked direction has residual geometric delay τ. Averaging its frequency-dependent phase over a top-hat band gives the displayed sinc attenuation times its central-frequency complex phase. The first bandwidth null is complete cancellation, not a small-loss operating limit. Fine frequency channels preserve the information needed for later frequency-aware imaging.
Primary beam (A(l,m))
Words: 47
Complex visibility OurBigBook.com
The primary beam is the individual antenna pair's directional sensitivity envelope in the complex visibility equation. For identical, identically pointed elements it is the individual element's power pattern. Its angular width sets the useful field of view; the much longer interferometric baselines set finer measured scales. The primary beam and the dirty beam describe different responses.
One-Mile Telescope
Words: 99
Aperture synthesis OurBigBook.com
The One-Mile Telescope used three steerable 60-foot dishes: two fixed, one rail-mounted. The movable–fixed pairs supplied two baselines simultaneously. Twelve-hour tracks at successive rail positions sampled projected spacings. Phase-switching receivers measured in-phase and quadrature correlations; adjustable delay and phase rotation compensated tracking.[ref]
The readout was correlation versus time. Reference-phase subtraction should leave constant point-source phase; position offsets produce predictable variation. A source near the field's declination supplies a collimation check. Structure, instrumental error and sampling artefacts need separating.[ref]
Dirty beam (B(θ))
Words: 489 Articles: 2
Aperture synthesis OurBigBook.com
The dirty beam is the point spread function obtained by directly inverting the weighted sampled complex visibilities. For sampling positions uk​ and nonnegative weights wk​ with W=∑k​wk​>0, choose
B(θ)=W1​∑k​wk​e2πiuk​θ,B(0)=1.
(60)
Include each uk​ with −uk​ and the same weight so that B is real. Its unit peak convention means that an isolated unit point source contributes a shifted unit-height response. It is not a unit-integral convention. Sparse sampling can leave substantial subsidiary peaks, even when the longest interferometric baseline is large.
Dirty image (ID​=I∗B)
Words: 409 Articles: 1
Dirty beam OurBigBook.com
The dirty image is the direct weighted inverse Fourier transform of the measured complex visibilities:
ID​(θ)=W1​∑k​wk​V(uk​)e2πiuk​θ=∑j​Ij​B(θ−θj​).
(61)
The final equality follows by substituting the point-source complex visibility and exchanging the finite sums. For continuous brightness it is a convolution with the dirty beam, with the primary beam included in the brightness when necessary. Negative values and subsidiary peaks can arise from that response even when every true source has positive strength.
Two-point-source aperture synthesis (V(u)=e2πiu(0.00625)+0.65e−2πiu(0.009375))
Words: 342
Dirty image OurBigBook.com
Choose two point-like astronomical sources with (θ1​,I1​)=(−0.00625,1) and (θ2​,I2​)=(0.009375,0.65), where the angles are in radians and strengths use arbitrary common units. Their separation is Δθ=0.015625 radians. These are invented model parameters, not historical measurements. Their complex visibility follows immediately from the preceding derivation, and its squared magnitude is
∣V(u)∣2=1+0.652+1.30cos(2πuΔθ).
(62)
At u=0, V=1.65; at u=400, V=−1+0.65i; at u=800, V=0.35. The unequal strengths prevent the complex visibility magnitude from reaching zero. Its modulation contains the source separation, while a common displacement of both sources changes wave phase without changing this magnitude. Amplitude alone loses that location information.
The sparse case samples u=±12.5k for k∈{2,5,9,14,20,28,36,44,52,60,64}; the denser case samples every k=1,…,64, also with both signs. All weights are one. Both reach ∣u∣=800, so their shortest fringe period is the same 0.00125 radians. Their dirty beams and false subsidiary features differ because the intermediate spatial frequencies differ. Neither case includes u=0 or frequencies above that maximum. The figure uses a periodic angular interval of length 0.08 radians; this artificial boundary makes a discrete Fourier transform calculation exact for the chosen grid, rather than modelling an all-sky observation.
The plotted dirty image is the sum of two shifted dirty beams, not a fitted or deconvolved estimate of the source. Adding samples in this example reduces prominent spurious peaks; it does not establish a universal monotonic improvement for every weighting or sky. A missing zero baseline leaves the periodic dirty image with zero mean, so it cannot by itself recover the total positive brightness. Missing short spacings also weaken constraints on extended smooth emission.
Reconstruction is an inverse problem. A perturbation whose Fourier transform vanishes at every sampled coordinate can be added without changing the measurements: incomplete coverage leaves a null space. Nonnegative brightness, a restricted source region, or a model with a small number of components can reduce ambiguity, but each is additional information. Removing dirty beam artefacts means estimating a sky consistent with both data and such assumptions; a narrow central peak alone does not certify a unique image. Measurement error, uncertain calibration and source variability add further limitations.

Flux-limited galaxy selection (Vmax​∝L3/2)

Words: 69
Observational astronomy OurBigBook.com
For a nearby Euclidean survey with limiting flux fmin​, a galaxy of luminosity L is detectable out to dmax​=L/(4πfmin​)​. Its accessible volume is therefore proportional to L3/2. With a Schechter function ϕ(L)∝Lαe−L/L∗​, counts per logarithmic interval are proportional to Lα+5/2e−L/L∗​ and peak at (α+5/2)L∗​ when α>−5/2. This selection suppresses faint objects relative to a volume-limited census; finite survey boundaries and cosmological evolution modify the simple law.

Angular resolution (θres​)

Words: 104 Articles: 1
Observational astronomy OurBigBook.com
Angular resolution describes the smallest angular separation or structure an observation can distinguish. A physical scale r at distance D subtends approximately r/D radians when r≪D. Resolving a black-hole sphere of influence therefore involves distance as well as its physical radius, and useful kinematics also require adequate surface brightness.

Retinal receptor pitch and angular sampling (θpitch​≃1/(fn​))

Words: 60
Angular resolution OurBigBook.com
For a roughly square array of retinal receptors with surface density n and image distance f, the pitch is s≃n−1/2 and its angular scale is s/f. Reconstructing a periodic spatial pattern requires at least two samples per period under the Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem. Receptor density alone does not specify lattice geometry, contrast sensitivity or a unique point-source resolution criterion.

Surface brightness (I)

Words: 367 Articles: 6
Observational astronomy OurBigBook.com
Surface brightness is received flux per unit solid angle on the sky. It describes the brightness of an extended source independently of a particular aperture's area. An isophote is a contour of constant surface brightness; central surface brightness sets the available photons for resolved galaxy spectroscopy.

Telescope aperture and resolved surface brightness (Atel​Ωres​∼λ2)

Words: 64
Surface brightness OurBigBook.com
For a diffraction-limited telescope, collecting area scales as D2 while a native angular resolution element scales as (λ/D)2. Counts from a smooth resolved source per native resolution element therefore do not increase with aperture, at fixed radiance, exposure and throughput. Counts in a fixed angular bin instead grow as D2, and the photon-noise-limited signal-to-noise ratio grows as Dt​. Conservation of etendue and cosmological surface-brightness dimming do not forbid this latter gain.

Cosmological surface-brightness dimming (Ibol,obs​=Ibol,em​/(1+z)4)

Words: 73
Surface brightness OurBigBook.com
For freely propagating radiation with the usual distance duality relation, a fixed emitted bolometric surface brightness is observed smaller by (1+z)4. One factor each comes from photon energy and arrival rate, and two from the relation of projected angular area to luminosity distance. In a fixed observed photometric passband, spectral shifts add a band-dependent correction; the bolometric power is not automatically the monochromatic one. A distortion created by scattering the local cosmic microwave background has a different redshift comparison, as in the thermal Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect.

Luminosity convergence of an outer surface-brightness profile (I(R)∝R−p:Louter​<∞⟺p>2)

Words: 69
Surface brightness OurBigBook.com
For a circular projected profile with a positive power-law tail, an annulus contributes dF=2πI(R)RdR. Thus the outer integral converges only when p>2; p=2 diverges logarithmically and p<2 as R2−p. A shallower tail measured over a finite range must steepen or terminate before an infinite-radius extrapolation is physical. This projected criterion already includes line-of-sight integration and must not be replaced by a three-dimensional r2dr volume factor.

Sérsic profile (I(R)=Ie​e−bn​[(R/Re​)1/n−1])

Words: 71 Articles: 1
Surface brightness OurBigBook.com
A Sérsic profile models projected galactic light, with index n controlling curvature and bn​ chosen so that Re​ encloses half the luminosity. Its logarithmic slope is dlnI/dlnR=−(bn​/n)(R/Re​)1/n. The n=1 case is exponential; n=4 gives the traditional de Vaucouleurs form. Unlike a fixed power law, its slope steepens outward.
de Vaucouleurs's law
Words: 22
Sérsic profile OurBigBook.com
The n=4 case of the Sérsic surface-brightness profile, approximately useful for many bright elliptical galaxies: I(R)=Ie​exp[−7.67((R/Re​)1/4−1)]. Real galaxies can have other Sérsic indices.

Projection of a spherical power-law emissivity (j∝r−p⟹I∝R1−p)

Words: 50
Surface brightness OurBigBook.com
An optically thin spherical source with volume emissivity j(r)=j0​r−p has surface brightness
I(R)=4πj0​​R1−pπ​Γ(p/2)Γ((p−1)/2)​,p>1.
(63)
Substitute z=Ru in the line-of-sight integral and evaluate ∫−∞∞​(1+u2)−p/2du using the beta function. The condition p>1 is convergence at large distance. A core or finite outer boundary changes the projection near that boundary; the stated scaling applies between those scales.

Isophote

Words: 90 Articles: 1
Observational astronomy OurBigBook.com
An isophote is a contour of equal surface brightness in an astronomical image. Deviations from fitted ellipses encode additional information about a galaxy's projected stellar structure.

Boxy and disky isophotes (a4​cos(4θ))

Words: 65
Isophote OurBigBook.com
Writing an isophote's radial residual about its fitted ellipse as δr=a4​cos4θ+⋯, positive a4​ extends the major and minor axes and gives a pointed, disky shape; negative a4​ extends diagonal directions and gives a boxy shape. The sign stated here is for radial residuals, not an unconverted brightness residual. Massive slowly rotating elliptical galaxies commonly have boxy isophotes, while embedded rotating disks commonly make lower-mass elliptical galaxies disky.

Sky brightness

Words: 33
Observational astronomy OurBigBook.com
Sky brightness is the diffuse radiance received away from an astronomical target. Ground-based observations include atmospheric airglow, scattered light, and thermal radiation; extraterrestrial diffuse light also contributes. Its photon fluctuations contribute to the signal-to-noise ratio in photon counting.
